title: System design: trust boundaries, SLOs and release evidence
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects system design: trust boundaries, slos and release evidence with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. Produce a design memo with requirements, architecture, sequence flow, tradeoffs, evaluation plan, load plan and failure matrix.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: AI system design begins with users, tasks, failure costs and measurable constraints. A support chatbot, failure triage service, test-generation platform and enterprise RAG system share components but have different permissions, latency and quality requirements. State what the system may decide autonomously and what requires review.
A diagram is useful when it shows data flow, trust boundaries, state and failure paths. Boxes named LLM and database alone do not explain authorization, freshness, budgets or recovery.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Design the shared quality platform with authenticated API, typed domain services, retrieval, bounded agent tools, evaluation runner and report storage. Keep provider credentials server-side, tenant filters before retrieval and writes behind concrete approval.

Specify SLOs for latency, accepted accuracy and availability, plus hard invariants for privacy and tool effects. Plan cache scope, queue capacity, trace correlation, index updates and compatible rollback. Compare a deterministic baseline before adding autonomous orchestration.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A design scales generation workers but ignores vector-store filtering and evaluator capacity. Another claims zero hallucinations without an evidence/abstention mechanism. A human approval box has no definition of the exact action being approved.

Walk through normal, ambiguous, malicious and outage requests. For each, identify state changes, budgets, authorization decisions and visible outcome. Check whether the same evidence can support a release and an incident investigation.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Produce a design memo with requirements, architecture, sequence flow, tradeoffs, evaluation plan, load plan and failure matrix. Demonstrate one complete request and one injected outage through the runnable platform.
SDETs should ask what evidence would disprove the design's claims. Every major guarantee should connect to a test, metric, policy boundary or operational procedure that can actually be inspected.

takeaway: Produce a design memo with requirements, architecture, sequence flow, tradeoffs, evaluation plan, load plan and failure matrix.

title: Phase 40 checkpoint: apply, break and evaluate
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions

relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects phase 40 checkpoint: apply, break and evaluate with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: This phase checkpoint connects system design: trust boundaries, slos and release evidence to the shared CI quality platform. Begin with the input contract, identify the expected output, and state which facts are known from fixtures versus inferred. Your task is to produce a reviewable decision, not merely repeat the definition.

Read the phase's worked examples before attempting the assessment. An accepted result must preserve authorized evidence, handle the demonstrated failure mode and explain what would invalidate the decision. Keep a field note containing the fixture ID and your reasoning.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Design the shared quality platform with authenticated API, typed domain services, retrieval, bounded agent tools, evaluation runner and report storage. Keep provider credentials server-side, tenant filters before retrieval and writes behind concrete approval.

Specify SLOs for latency, accepted accuracy and availability, plus hard invariants for privacy and tool effects. Plan cache scope, queue capacity, trace correlation, index updates and compatible rollback. Compare a deterministic baseline before adding autonomous orchestration.

Apply this mechanism to a synthetic incident in the shared fixture set. Preserve input/output identities so a reviewer can reproduce the result. Use the earlier lessons' implementation checks rather than assuming the checkpoint example is correct.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A design scales generation workers but ignores vector-store filtering and evaluator capacity. Another claims zero hallucinations without an evidence/abstention mechanism. A human approval box has no definition of the exact action being approved.

Walk through normal, ambiguous, malicious and outage requests. For each, identify state changes, budgets, authorization decisions and visible outcome. Check whether the same evidence can support a release and an incident investigation.

Construct a counterexample that fails the intended invariant, then describe how the same test would catch a future regression. State which layer owns the correction: data, numerical code, API validation, retrieval, policy or evaluation.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Produce a design memo with requirements, architecture, sequence flow, tradeoffs, evaluation plan, load plan and failure matrix. Demonstrate one complete request and one injected outage through the runnable platform.
SDETs should ask what evidence would disprove the design's claims. Every major guarantee should connect to a test, metric, policy boundary or operational procedure that can actually be inspected.

The checkpoint memo is assessed with an explicit evidence checklist. Its keyword checks confirm required topics are present; they do not establish the technical truth of your design. Review the worked approach and retain executable evidence where the phase includes code.

takeaway: Produce a design memo with requirements, architecture, sequence flow, tradeoffs, evaluation plan, load plan and failure matrix.

exercise.prompt: Apply System design: trust boundaries, SLOs and release evidence to a synthetic CI incident. Write a memo with the input contract, an implementation decision, a failure counterexample, a test/evaluation result, and a release or review decision.
exercise.solution:
Start with an input contract tied to a fixture ID. Explain the implementation using the phase mechanism. Provide evidence from a behavior check or evaluated example. Include a failure counterexample and the test that catches it. Finish with a release or review decision justified by the stated evidence.

Produce a design memo with requirements, architecture, sequence flow, tradeoffs, evaluation plan, load plan and failure matrix.

quiz.question: A candidate for system design: trust boundaries, slos and release evidence meets the happy path but fails the phase's documented counterexample. What is the defensible decision?
options: Hold release, preserve the failing case and fix the responsible boundary
Release because the happy path passed
Delete the failing case to improve the score
quiz.explanation: The failing counterexample disproves the claimed contract. Retain it as regression evidence and rerun the corrected boundary.
